describe: Turn off SMBv1 (obsolete file-sharing protocol) -- risk: Very old NAS boxes, scanners or Windows XP-era PCs that only speak SMBv1 can no longer connect.
Turn off LLMNR name lookups -- risk: Single-word names that only resolve through LLMNR stop resolving on networks without proper DNS.

Turn off AutoRun and AutoPlay on every drive type -- risk: Inserted USB sticks and discs no longer start installers or show the AutoPlay prompt, and phones and cameras no longer show the import-photos prompt; open them from File Explorer.

Windows Firewall on for all network profiles, inbound blocked unless a rule allows it -- risk: A program that must accept incoming connections (game server, file sharing, remote tools) needs an allow rule. The script runs once at the end of Setup and does not retry; the log says [WARN] if the firewall settings are not in effect.

Defender: block potentially unwanted apps and turn cloud protection on -- risk: Some bundled freeware may be flagged, and cloud protection sends file metadata to Microsoft. The script runs once at the end of Setup and does not retry; Tamper Protection, another antivirus or a Defender that is not ready yet can stop the change, and the log then says [WARN].

Defender attack surface rule in Block mode: no credential stealing from LSASS -- risk: Rarely, security or backup tools that read LSASS memory are blocked and Defender shows a notification. The script runs once at the end of Setup and does not retry; the log says [WARN] if the rule is not in effect.

Defender attack surface rules in Audit mode (log only): email executable content, Office child processes, obfuscated scripts, script-launched downloads -- risk: Audit mode only writes events and blocks nothing. Review the Defender event log before switching any rule to Block. The script runs once at the end of Setup and does not retry; the log says [WARN] for a rule that is not in effect.

Defender attack surface rules in Audit mode (log only), more: abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers, process creation from PsExec and WMI commands, untrusted processes that run from USB drives -- risk: Audit mode only writes events and blocks nothing; running programs from a USB stick or with remote-management tools adds events. Review the Defender event log before switching any rule to Block. The script runs once at the end of Setup and does not retry; the log says [WARN] for a rule that is not in effect.
Do not keep plain-text WDigest credentials in memory -- risk: Only legacy digest authentication against very old web servers is affected.
PowerShell script block logging -- risk: Adds events to the PowerShell log; secrets typed inside a script would be logged as well.
Disable the PowerShell 2.0 optional feature -- risk: Very old scripts or tools that insist on running with -Version 2 stop working.
Turn off Remote Assistance invitations -- risk: Old-style Remote Assistance invitations stop working; Quick Assist and Remote Desktop are not changed.

Advanced audit policy: sign-ins, account lockouts, account and group changes, audit-policy changes, process creation; Security log size raised to 128 MiB -- risk: The Security event log fills much faster (process creation and sign-ins are frequent events), so its maximum size is raised to 128 MiB (never lowered). Retention is still limited: on a busy PC the oldest events can be overwritten within days, so export the log if you need to keep it.
Keep User Account Control switched on -- risk: Only acts when UAC was switched off; takes effect after the next restart.

Opt-in (-DisableLegacyNetwork, never applied by default): turn off NetBIOS over TCP/IP on all network adapters -- risk: Looking up or browsing machines by their NetBIOS name stops working on the adapters that exist now (very old file shares, printers or NAS boxes reached by a short name). It takes effect when the adapter reconnects or after a restart; adapters added later keep their default.

Opt-in (-DisableLegacyNetwork, never applied by default): turn off WPAD proxy auto-discovery for WinHTTP -- risk: A network that hands out its proxy only through WPAD (some offices and schools) no longer gives it to Windows services and apps that use WinHTTP, so they can lose internet access until a proxy is set by hand. The WinHTTP auto-proxy service itself is left running.
